key_terms.meaning: Learning from data with no target label; the goal is to describe structure, groups or compressed features.
Grouping points so that points in one group are more similar to each other than to points outside it.
d = √Σ(xᵢ − yᵢ)² over all features i; straight-line distance.
d = Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|; distance travelled along feature axes, less sensitive to big single differences.
Hard gives each point one cluster; soft gives a degree or probability for every cluster.
The mean vector of all points currently in a cluster; its coordinates are the average of each feature.
J = Σ over clusters Σ over points in the cluster ‖x − μ‖²; the quantity k-means minimises.
Bottom-up hierarchical method: start with n singleton clusters and repeatedly merge the two closest.
Tree diagram whose vertical axis shows the distance at which two clusters were merged or split.
Rule for the distance between two clusters: single (closest pair), complete (farthest pair), average, or Ward.
p(x) = Σₖ πₖ N(x | μₖ, Σₖ), a weighted sum of k Gaussian components with weights πₖ summing to 1.
Iterative fitting for models with hidden variables: E-step computes responsibilities, M-step re-estimates parameters.
A direction (unit vector) in feature space along which the projected data has maximum variance, orthogonal to earlier ones.
λᵢ ÷ Σλ, the share of total variance carried by principal component i.
Keeping a subset of the original features and discarding the rest, so the model stays interpretable.
r = cov(X,Y) ÷ (σ_X σ_Y), between −1 and +1; near 0 means little linear relation.
Supervised projection that maximises between-class scatter S_B relative to within-class scatter S_W.
s = (b − a) ÷ max(a, b), where a is mean distance to own cluster and b to the nearest other cluster; range −1 to 1.
Fraction of point pairs on which predicted and true groupings agree (both together or both apart).
In fuzzy clustering, uᵢⱼ ∈ [0, 1] giving how strongly point i belongs to cluster j, with Σⱼ uᵢⱼ = 1.

takeaways: Unsupervised learning has no labels, so the distance or similarity you choose decides what a cluster means.
K-means alternates assign and update steps to reduce WCSS; it is fast but needs k in advance and assumes round, similar-sized clusters.
Hierarchical clustering builds a whole tree at once, so you can cut it at any height and read the merges from a dendrogram.
A Gaussian mixture is a soft, model-based version of k-means that allows elliptical clusters of different size and orientation.
EM fits a mixture by repeating two steps: estimate hidden memberships, then re-estimate parameters from those memberships.
PCA rotates the axes to the directions of maximum variance, so a few components can replace many correlated features.
Feature selection keeps original columns while PCA creates new ones; correlation analysis is the quick test for redundant columns.
LDA uses class labels to find a projection that separates classes, and gives at most c − 1 components for c classes.
Clustering quality is judged by cohesion and separation when no labels exist, and by agreement scores when labels do exist.
Fuzzy clustering replaces the single assignment with membership degrees, which suits data where clusters overlap.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually asked as full algorithm descriptions with a worked small example plus a comparison table, so practise k-means, hierarchical, GMM/EM, PCA, LDA and clustering evaluation as numbered procedures.

bank.q: Define unsupervised learning. Explain the main types of clustering (partitional vs hierarchical, hard vs soft, density-based vs model-based) and the distance measures used to decide similarity.
outline: Unsupervised learning: only input data X, no y; aim is structure, grouping or compression.
Partitional gives a flat set of k groups; hierarchical gives a nested tree; density-based grows regions of high point density; model-based assumes a probability model per cluster.
Hard assignment: one cluster per point. Soft: membership values or probabilities.
Euclidean distance formula and when it suits continuous features; Manhattan distance and when it is preferred (outliers, grid-like data).
Scaling of features matters because distance is not scale-free.

bank.q: Describe the k-means clustering algorithm. State its objective function, the steps, the stopping rule and its main limitations.
outline: Objective: minimise WCSS J = Σₖ Σ_{x in Cₖ} ‖x − μₖ‖².

Step 1: choose k and initial centroids. Step 2: assign each point to the nearest centroid. Step 3: recompute each centroid as the mean of its points. Repeat until assignments stop changing or J stops falling.
Complexity per iteration O(n · k · d) for n points, d features.
Limitations: k must be fixed in advance, result depends on initialisation, sensitive to outliers, assumes roughly spherical equal-size clusters, only finds local minima.
Fixes: k-means++ initialisation, several restarts, elbow method or silhouette to choose k.

bank.q: Explain hierarchical clustering. Distinguish agglomerative and divisive approaches, describe linkage rules, and explain how a dendrogram is read.
outline: Agglomerative: bottom-up, start with n singleton clusters, merge the closest pair repeatedly, O(n³) naive or better with priority queues.
Divisive: top-down, start with one cluster, split repeatedly; more expensive because all splits must be considered.
Linkage: single (minimum pair distance), complete (maximum), average, centroid, Ward (minimum increase in WCSS).
Distance matrix updated after each merge; cut the dendrogram at a chosen height to get the final clusters.
Single linkage can chain; complete and Ward give more compact clusters.

bank.q: Explain the Gaussian mixture model and derive the EM updates used to fit it.
outline: Model: p(x) = Σₖ πₖ N(x | μₖ, Σₖ), with πₖ ≥ 0 and Σπₖ = 1.
Hidden variable z says which component produced a point; log-likelihood with hidden z cannot be maximised directly.
E-step: responsibility rᵢₖ = πₖ N(xᵢ | μₖ, Σₖ) ÷ Σⱼ πⱼ N(xᵢ | μⱼ, Σⱼ).
M-step: Nₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ, πₖ = Nₖ/n, μₖ = (1/Nₖ) Σᵢ rᵢₖ xᵢ, Σₖ = (1/Nₖ) Σᵢ rᵢₖ (xᵢ − μₖ)(xᵢ − μₖ)ᵀ.
Each iteration increases the log-likelihood; stop when the increase is below a tolerance.

bank.q: Given the points (1,1), (2,1), (4,3), (5,4) with initial centroids μ₁ = (1,1) and μ₂ = (5,4), run two full iterations of k-means using Euclidean distance and show the final clusters and WCSS.
outline: Iteration 1: compute squared distances from each point to both centroids and assign to the nearer one.
Recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points.
Iteration 2: reassign with the new centroids, recompute centroids, check that assignments are unchanged.
Compute WCSS as the sum of squared distances from each point to its own centroid.
State the stopping condition clearly and show all arithmetic.

bank.q: For the points A(1,2), B(2,1), C(5,6), D(6,5), E(1,1), build the Euclidean distance matrix and carry out agglomerative clustering with single linkage until two clusters remain. Draw the dendrogram.
outline: Compute pairwise Euclidean distances, e.g. d(A,B) = √2, and tabulate them.
First merge the closest pair (A and E, or A and B); show the distance.
Update the distance matrix using the single-linkage rule: distance between merged cluster and another point is the minimum of the two distances.
Continue merging and record the merge heights.
Draw the dendrogram with merge height on the vertical axis and label the cut that gives two clusters.

bank.q: A two-feature data set has covariance matrix S = [[4, 2], [2, 3]]. Find the principal components, the explained variance ratio and the projection of the point (1, 1).
outline: Eigenvalues from det(S − λI) = 0: λ² − 7λ + 8 = 0, so λ = (7 ± √17)/2.
Eigenvector for each λ from (S − λI)v = 0; normalise to unit length and check orthogonality.
Explained variance ratio = λ₁ ÷ (λ₁ + λ₂) for the first component.
Centre the point (subtract the feature means) before projecting, then take dot products with the two eigenvectors.
State that PCA components are orthogonal and ordered by variance.

bank.q: A data set has features F1, F2, F3, F4. The correlation matrix shows r(F1,F2) = 0.95, r(F3,F4) = 0.08, r(F1,F3) = 0.11. Explain how you would use this to select features, and how forward selection and backward elimination would proceed.
outline: Highly correlated pair F1, F2 carries almost the same information; drop one, keeping the one with higher correlation to the target or lower missing-value rate.
F3 and F4 are nearly independent, so both may be kept if each is useful.
Forward selection: start empty, add the feature that improves validation score most, repeat until no gain.
Backward elimination: start with all features, remove the least useful, repeat.
Always judge on validation data, not training data, to avoid overfitting.

bank.q: Compare k-means and a Gaussian mixture model for the same data set. Explain when k-means gives wrong groupings and how GMM fixes that, including the cost paid.
outline: Both are partitional and alternate two steps; k-means is the hard-assignment special case of GMM with equal spherical covariances.
k-means fails when clusters are elongated, of very different sizes, or overlapping, because it uses only distance to the centroid.
GMM learns full covariance matrices, so clusters can be elliptical and tilted; responsibilities give soft memberships.
Cost: more parameters to estimate, slower, needs more data per component, can converge to a local maximum or a singular covariance.
Choose by the problem: quick segmentation on scaled round clusters favours k-means; overlapping density structure favours GMM.

bank.q: Compare PCA and LDA for dimensionality reduction. Why is LDA limited to c − 1 components, and when would you prefer PCA?
outline: PCA is unsupervised: it maximises total variance, ignores labels, components are orthogonal eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.
LDA is supervised: it maximises S_B relative to S_W, so it keeps directions that separate classes and can discard high-variance directions that mix classes.
S_B is a sum of c rank-one terms built from c class means, and after centring its rank is at most c − 1, so LDA gives at most c − 1 useful directions.
LDA needs labelled data and enough samples per class to estimate S_W; it assumes shared covariance across classes.
Prefer PCA for compression, visualisation or unlabelled data; prefer LDA when labels exist and the goal is classification.

bank.q: How do you evaluate a clustering result? Explain internal measures (WCSS, silhouette, Davies–Bouldin), external measures (Rand index, purity) and the elbow method.
outline: No target label exists, so quality must come from cohesion inside clusters and separation between them.
WCSS falls as k grows, so it cannot pick k alone; use the elbow where the fall flattens.
Silhouette: a = mean distance to own cluster members, b = mean distance to nearest other cluster, s = (b − a) ÷ max(a, b); mean s over points, higher is better.
External measures need true labels: Rand index counts agreeing pairs; purity is the fraction of points matching the majority class of their cluster.
Report the metric with the distance used and with features scaled, since all these scores depend on the distance.

bank.q: Explain fuzzy c-means clustering. Give the objective function and update equations, compare it with k-means, and state one practical use of the membership values.
outline: Objective J = Σᵢ Σⱼ uᵢⱼᵐ ‖xᵢ − cⱼ‖², with m > 1 the fuzzifier, uᵢⱼ ∈ [0,1] and Σⱼ uᵢⱼ = 1 for each point.
Update: cⱼ = Σᵢ uᵢⱼᵐ xᵢ ÷ Σᵢ uᵢⱼᵐ and uᵢⱼ = 1 ÷ Σₖ (‖xᵢ − cⱼ‖ ÷ ‖xᵢ − cₖ‖)^(2/(m−1)).
As m → 1 the solution approaches hard k-means; large m makes memberships near 1/c.
Comparison: fuzzy is softer and handles overlapping clusters, but costs more computation and you still fix c.
Use: points with mid-range memberships are ambiguous cases, e.g. a customer whose spending sits between two segments, flagged for manual review.

bank.q: A payments company wants to segment users from UPI transaction data with 40 numeric features. Design the full pipeline: preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, choice of clustering method, choosing k, and evaluation.
outline: Preprocess: handle missing values, remove or cap outliers, standardise each feature to zero mean and unit variance because distances are scale dependent.
Reduce: drop near-constant and near-duplicate features by correlation analysis; then apply PCA and keep enough components for about 90% explained variance.
Cluster: k-means with k-means++ and several restarts on scaled or PCA features; compare with hierarchical clustering on a sample and with GMM if segments may overlap.
Choose k by elbow of WCSS and peak mean silhouette; check that segments are large enough to act on.
Evaluate with silhouette and Davies–Bouldin, then validate business meaning by profiling each segment; watch that PCA components are combinations and need interpretation.

glossary.def: A set of data points judged more similar to each other than to points outside the set.
A function giving a non-negative similarity gap between two points, satisfying symmetry and the triangle inequality.
In many dimensions, distances between points become nearly equal, so clustering and nearest-neighbour methods lose power.
Initialisation that picks the first centroid at random and later ones with probability proportional to squared distance from the nearest chosen centroid.
Plotting WCSS against k and choosing the k where the curve stops falling steeply.
The vector of feature-wise means of the points in a cluster.
The actual data point of a cluster that has the smallest total distance to the other members.
Cluster distance taken as the smallest distance between any member of one cluster and any member of the other.
Merge rule that picks the pair whose merging causes the smallest increase in total within-cluster sum of squares.
A horizontal line drawn across the tree; the number of branches it crosses is the number of clusters returned.
The posterior probability that a given point was generated by a particular mixture component.
The weight πₖ of component k in a mixture, equal to the prior probability that a random point comes from it.
A square matrix whose entry (i, j) is the covariance between features i and j; its diagonal holds the variances.
A scalar λ for which S v = λ v has a non-zero solution v; for a covariance matrix it equals the variance along v.
A non-zero direction v that a matrix only stretches, not rotates, when multiplied.
At right angles, meaning the dot product of the two vectors is zero.
Scaling PCA components to unit variance so the transformed features are uncorrelated and equally spread.
A bar or line chart of the eigenvalues in decreasing order, used to decide how many components to keep.
Strong correlation among input features, which makes regression coefficients unstable and hard to interpret.
External clustering score equal to the total, over clusters, of the majority-class count divided by n.
Average over clusters of the ratio of within-cluster spread to distance between cluster centres; lower is better.
The exponent m > 1 in fuzzy c-means that controls how much overlap between clusters is allowed.
Turning membership degrees into a single decision, usually by assigning each point to the cluster with the highest membership.
Clustering that grows clusters as connected regions having at least a minimum number of points within a radius, and marks the rest as noise.
